items.stem: A platform team must connect the agent to the organization's issue-tracking system used company-wide. An actively maintained community MCP server already exposes the equivalent operations, and a custom build needs three engineer-weeks requiring the engineering director's approval. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Build a custom MCP server duplicating the tracker's full API surface, spending the approved three-week budget.
Call the tracker directly from the orchestration layer on every request, bypassing model discretion.
Reject the community server as unreliable and commission a custom build, citing a lack of maintenance.
Adopt the actively maintained community MCP server instead of building a custom integration.

items.whyRight: A community MCP server already exposes the tracker's standard operations and is actively maintained, so custom effort should go where nothing else covers the workflow, without spending the approved budget or the director's time on infrastructure that already exists.

whyWrong.A: Building a custom server duplicates functionality an actively maintained community option already provides, spending scarce build budget on a solved problem this section reserves for genuinely unique workflows.
whyWrong.B: Direct orchestration-layer calls suit a mandatory step that must run on every request; connecting to a standard third-party system is a build-versus-adopt decision, not that one.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the server is actively maintained, which directly contradicts the claim of unreliable upkeep used to justify commissioning a custom build instead.

items.t1Clause: an actively maintained community MCP server already exposes the equivalent operations

items.stem: A production agent needs the same 4,000-token compliance policy block on every request, at 200,000 requests/day under a strict p95 latency SLA. An engineer proposes moving it into the progressive-discovery index so it loads only when needed. What should the architect decide?

opts.t: Move the block into the progressive-discovery index and fetch it with an extra model turn per request.
Expose it as a namespace-level index entry with on-demand expansion, matching the pattern for large tool surfaces.
Remove the block from the base prompt and rely on the model to request it only for compliance queries.
Keep the block ordered first in the base prompt, with prompt caching enabled.

items.whyRight: The block is required on every request, so nothing is actually being discovered; ordering it first and caching the prefix removes its latency cost without adding a round-trip that a fetch-on-demand design would introduce at this volume.

whyWrong.A: Fetching the block on demand adds a model turn to a request that always needs it, spending the round-trip cost this pattern exists to avoid.
whyWrong.B: Namespace indexing suits a large surface where most content is irrelevant to a given request; this block is required by every single request, so no expansion decision applies.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the block is needed on every request; skipping it and hoping the model asks for it risks compliance content being silently absent.

items.t1Clause: needs the same 4,000-token compliance policy block on every request
items.factAnswerRaw: Order it first with prompt caching

items.stem: A teammate argues the multi-tenant assistant runs under one trusted, internal service account, so per-user access control is already handled at a shared tiered document store serving 40,000 requests/day; auditors require enforcement provable at the point of access. Select the two corrections required.

opts.t: Propagate each requesting user's identity into the retrieval layer, replacing reliance on the shared service account alone.
Add a system-prompt instruction naming which tiers the agent may cite, leaving the shared account unchanged.
Apply the entitlement filter inside the retrieval query itself, before content is ranked or returned.
Replace the shared token with per-user credentials, though attribution to an outside operator was never required.

items.whyRight: The service account collapses every user into one identity at the point data is reached, so entitlement has to be re-established there: propagating the caller's identity and enforcing the filter inside the query are two separate, jointly required steps auditors can point to as proof.

whyWrong.B: A system-prompt rule is a probabilistic instruction the model might not follow; auditors need enforcement that is structurally deterministic, not asserted in a prompt.
whyWrong.D: Per-user credential substitution answers a third-party attribution requirement; this store is internal, so it adds credential-management overhead the situation does not call for.

items.stem: A nightly reconciliation pipeline processes 50,000 records against a 90-minute p95 SLA, consistently missing it. It parses each complete model response before writing downstream, and an engineer proposes enabling streaming to fix the miss. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Enable streaming and report the improved time-to-first-token against the 90-minute SLA.
Reject streaming for this consumer and reduce total latency at the pipeline's slowest measured stage.
Enable streaming and report the nightly run's improved mean latency, leaving the p95 figure unchanged.
Add a monitoring alert that flags SLA breaches after each nightly run, leaving the pipeline unchanged.

items.whyRight: The pipeline waits for each complete response before writing downstream, so time-to-first-token never mattered here; total latency is unchanged by streaming, and the SLA breach can only close by reducing time at the slowest measured stage.

whyWrong.A: Time-to-first-token only matters to a consumer reading incrementally; this pipeline waits for the complete response, so the reported metric never touches the SLA it actually misses.
whyWrong.C: A mean-latency improvement can hide an unchanged p95, which is the percentile the 90-minute SLA actually names; streaming still buys nothing for a consumer waiting on the full response.
whyWrong.D: Flagging breaches after each run confirms the SLA was missed again; it does nothing to shorten the pipeline's slowest stage, which is what the miss is caused by.

items.t1Clause: parses each complete model response before writing downstream

items.stem: A team investigating an intermittent tool-call failure affecting under 1% of 500,000 daily requests proposes capturing full-fidelity traces for all traffic "temporarily, until the cause is found," though the data includes regulated customer records. What should the architect decide?

opts.t: Approve full-fidelity capture for two weeks across all traffic, then revert to the prior policy.
Take a small uniform sample of routine successes for a baseline, leaving error paths unsampled.
Log full request and response payloads for every trace, since this data is central to the diagnosis.
Reject full-fidelity capture; stratify at 100% for errors and low-confidence paths, with redacted metadata for regulated access.

items.whyRight: At this volume the failure is rare, so it needs its own 100% stratum rather than a slice of routine traffic; full-fidelity capture of everything is unaffordable here and duplicates regulated records into a second sensitive store.

whyWrong.A: A two-week window still captures full-fidelity traces of regulated records at this volume; deferring the cost and exposure decision does not remove either one.
whyWrong.B: A uniform sample of routine successes serves baseline detection, not diagnosing a rare failure; leaving error paths unsampled misses the exact events under investigation.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the data includes regulated customer records, which requires redacted payload at the point of access, not full unredacted request and response logging.

items.factAnswerRaw: Reject on cost and on data-protection exposure

items.stem: A policy-document RAG pipeline already contextualizes each chunk with its title and heading path before embedding, sized to answer multi-sentence questions. Finance wants chunk size cut further to reduce a rising embedding bill. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Shrink the chunk size as finance requests, since embedding cost scales directly with size.
Keep the current chunk size and contextualization, and reject the proposed further shrink.
Shrink the chunks but prepend an even longer heading path to compensate for the loss.
Fix the chunk boundaries to follow the document's structure instead of changing the size.

items.whyRight: The chunks are already sized correctly and contextualized for multi-sentence questions; shrinking further to cut cost would remove content those questions depend on. The stated requirement to retain enough surrounding context outranks an unstated cost target, so the current sizing stays.

whyWrong.A: Embedding cost does scale with size, but shrinking below what multi-sentence questions need breaks the stated context requirement to chase an unstated cost target.
whyWrong.C: A longer heading path adds context about structure, not the surrounding content a shrunken chunk just lost; the multi-sentence answer still is not there to retrieve.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the stem indicates the chunks are truncated or cut mid-idea; boundary structure is not the problem finance is asking to solve here.

items.t1Clause: to reduce a rising embedding bill
items.factAnswerRaw: Keep the current chunk size and contextualization, and reject the proposed further shrink.

Kept facet:'M-3.3' per assignment and direction:normal per the misconception rule.
